opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that data is really the bottleneck in robotics. In language and vision, we've had the internet: this huge, naturally occurring corpus of text and images. Robotics doesn't have that. Every robot dataset is collected by someone, on a specific robot, in a specific lab or setting, and each one on its own is pretty small. So if you limit yourself to data from a single platform, you're stuck with a very narrow slice of experience, and it's hard to get the kind of breadth that leads to generalization.

When you pool data across many robots, you suddenly have much more diversity: different environments, different objects, different tasks, different ways of approaching the same problem. Even though the robots have different arms, grippers, cameras, and control schemes, a lot of the underlying structure is shared. How to approach a drawer, what it means to grasp a cup, how objects respond when you push them. That knowledge transfers. We saw this in efforts like Open X-Embodiment, where training on data from lots of different robots actually improved performance on individual robots compared to training only on that robot's own data. That was a really encouraging result, because it wasn't obvious ahead of time that the heterogeneity wouldn't hurt.

There's also a longer-term argument. If we want robots that can operate in the messy, open-ended real world, we can't build a separate model for every new piece of hardware and collect everything from scratch each time. Hardware is going to keep changing, and we want a model that can be adapted to a new robot quickly, maybe with a small amount of data. Training across embodiments pushes the model to learn representations that are less tied to one specific body, and that's what makes adapting to new platforms feasible.

So it's partly a scale argument, getting more data, and partly a generality argument: the diversity itself is what teaches the model to generalize. I think that combination is a big part of the path toward generalist robots, much like broad data was key for foundation models in other domains.

r001.rationale: The response says that shared knowledge about tasks and objects transfers across robots with different hardware and control schemes.

r002.rationale: It says hardware will keep changing and argues that training across embodiments lets a model adapt to new robots without collecting everything from scratch, so earlier data remains useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that data is the bottleneck. If you look at what's driven progress in language and vision, it's been models trained on enormous, diverse datasets scraped from the internet. Robotics doesn't have an internet of robot experience. Every robot that exists has collected a relatively tiny amount of data, and most of that data lives in silos, on one robot, in one lab, doing one set of tasks.

So if you're a single lab, and you want to train a policy for your robot, you might collect a few thousand demonstrations. That's enough to get something that works in your lab, on your table, with your objects, but it falls apart the moment the lighting changes or you move to a different building. Diversity is what gives you generalization, and no single lab or single platform is going to collect enough diversity on its own.

The question we had with the Open X-Embodiment effort was whether you could pool data across many different robots, with different arms, different grippers, different camera placements, different action spaces, and actually get a benefit from that, rather than just noise. And the somewhat surprising answer was yes. When we trained on data from twenty-some different robot types, the resulting policy outperformed policies trained only on the target robot's own data, even when evaluated on that robot. So the data from other embodiments wasn't just not hurting, it was actively helping.

I think the intuition for why that works is that a lot of what the model needs to learn is shared. How objects behave, what a grasp looks like, how to approach a drawer handle, how to recover when something slips. Those things are fairly platform-independent at the level of visual understanding, even if the low-level motor commands differ. And it turns out these models are pretty good at figuring out which parts transfer and which parts are specific to a given robot.

There's also just a practical, community-level argument. If every group is collecting data in isolation, we're collectively wasting an enormous amount of effort. If we can agree on formats and share, then the whole field benefits in the same way the vision community benefited from ImageNet. We're not at ImageNet scale yet for robotics, but I think cross-embodiment data is how we get there.

r001.rationale: The response says data from other robot embodiments actively helps and describes shared knowledge transferring despite differences in arms, grippers, cameras, and action spaces.

r002.rationale: It discusses pooling data across different robot hardware, but does not say that previously collected data remains useful after a robot’s hardware is revised.

astra-6.text:
If we want robots to generalize, they need to learn from a really broad range of experiences. And today, any individual robot platform has a pretty limited amount of data. If every time we build a new robot we have to collect all of its training data from scratch, it’s going to be very hard to scale.

What’s exciting is that a lot of the underlying knowledge should transfer across platforms. Two robots might have different arms or different grippers, but they’re both interacting with the same physical world. They both need to understand what objects are, how they move, and what happens when you push or grasp something.

Of course, you can’t necessarily send the same motor commands to both robots. The challenge is learning what’s shared while accounting for those differences. If we can do that, then data collected on one robot can help another robot learn, and a new platform can build on that experience instead of starting from zero.

r001.rationale: The response says knowledge transfers across platforms and data collected on one robot can help another robot learn.

r002.rationale: It discusses different robot hardware and new platforms building on prior experience, but does not clearly state that collected data remains useful after revisions to a robot’s hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that any individual robot is only going to collect a limited amount of experience. If we want robots that can generalize to new tasks and new environments, we need to be able to learn from experience collected across lots of different robots, even when they have different bodies or different sensors.

There’s a lot of shared structure in what those robots are doing. The way you interact with an object, or recognize that something can be picked up, isn’t completely different just because you have a different gripper. So the hope is that you can share that knowledge while still accounting for the specifics of each robot’s body and how it takes actions.

That also gives us a much better path to scale. Instead of every lab or company having to start from scratch with its own dataset, each robot can benefit from what other robots have learned.

r001.rationale: It says robots can learn from experience across different bodies and sensors, sharing knowledge while accounting for each robot’s specifics.

r002.rationale: It discusses sharing data across different robots, but does not state that previously collected data remains useful after a robot’s hardware is revised.
